title: Cardinality

When do two sets have the same size? For finite sets we can count; in general, we compare sets by means of maps between them.

:::definition{1.7.1} Cardinality
Sets $X$ and $Y$ have the ***same cardinality***, written $|X| = |Y|$, if there exists a bijection $X\to Y$. We write $|X|\le|Y|$ if there exists an injection $X\injto Y$, and $|X|<|Y|$ if $|X|\le|Y|$ and $|X|\neq|Y|$.
:::

These are relations between sets; we do not define $|X|$ as an object in its own right, except for finite sets. A set $X$ is ***finite*** if $|X| = |\{1,\ldots,n\}|$ for some $n\in\NN$ (where $\{1,\ldots,0\} = \emptyset$); this $n$ is unique, since an induction on $n$ shows that there is no injection $\{1,\ldots,n+1\}\injto\{1,\ldots,n\}$, and we write $|X| = n$, the number of elements of $X$. A set $X$ with $|X| = |\NN|$ is ***countably infinite***; a set that is finite or countably infinite is ***countable***; any other set is ***uncountable***.

Having the same cardinality behaves like an equivalence relation: $\id_X$ is a bijection, the inverse of a bijection is a bijection, and a composite of bijections is a bijection (Propositions [1.5.5](/notes/math-55a/1-5-inverses-and-composites#proposition-1-5-5) and [1.5.6](/notes/math-55a/1-5-inverses-and-composites#proposition-1-5-6)). Likewise $|X|\le|X|$, and $|X|\le|Y|\le|Z|$ implies $|X|\le|Z|$, since a composite of injections is injective. If $X\subseteq Y$, the inclusion map shows that $|X|\le|Y|$. The notation $\le$ is justified by the following theorem, which lets us relate cardinality and maps between sets.

:::theorem{1.7.2} Schröder–Bernstein
If there exist injections $f : X\injto Y$ and $g : Y\injto X$, then $|X| = |Y|$.
:::

:::proof
We build a bijection $h : X\to Y$ that uses $f$ on part of $X$ and the inverse of $g$ on the rest. Since $g$ is injective, every $x\in g(Y)$ is $g(y)$ for exactly one $y\in Y$, which we denote $g^{-1}(x)$.

Define subsets $C_0,C_1,C_2,\ldots$ of $X$ by $C_0 = X-g(Y)$ and $C_{k+1} = g(f(C_k))$, and let $C = \bigcup_{k\in\NN}C_k$. Every $x\in X-C$ lies outside $C_0$, so $x\in g(Y)$. Hence $$h(x) = \begin{cases} f(x) & \text{if } x\in C,\\ g^{-1}(x) & \text{if } x\in X-C \end{cases}$$ defines a function $h : X\to Y$.

*The map $h$ is injective.* Let $x\neq x'$. If both lie in $C$, then $h(x) = f(x)\neq f(x') = h(x')$. If neither does, then $h(x) = g^{-1}(x)$ and $h(x') = g^{-1}(x')$ are distinct, since $g$ sends them to $x$ and $x'$. Suppose $x\in C$ and $x'\notin C$, say $x\in C_k$. If $h(x) = h(x')$, then $f(x) = g^{-1}(x')$, so $x' = g(f(x))\in g(f(C_k)) = C_{k+1}\subseteq C$, a contradiction.

*The map $h$ is surjective.* Let $y\in Y$. If $g(y)\notin C$, then $h(g(y)) = g^{-1}(g(y)) = y$. If $g(y)\in C$, then $g(y)\notin C_0$, because $g(y)\in g(Y)$; so $g(y)\in C_{k+1} = g(f(C_k))$ for some $k$, and there is an $x\in C_k$ with $g(y) = g(f(x))$. Since $g$ is injective, $y = f(x) = h(x)$.
:::

:::note
The set $C$ has a simple description. Start from a point $x_0\in X$ that is not in the image of $g$ and follow the chain $x_0\mapsto f(x_0)\mapsto g(f(x_0))\mapsto f(g(f(x_0)))\mapsto\cdots$; then $C$ consists of the points of $X$ reached by such chains. On these points $h$ follows $f$ forward, and everywhere else $h$ follows $g$ backward.
:::

Several sets that look larger than $\NN$ turn out to have the same cardinality.

:::proposition{1.7.3} The integers are countable
The map $f : \ZZ\to\NN$ given by $$f(n) = \begin{cases} 2n & \text{if } n\ge 0,\\ -(2n+1) & \text{if } n<0 \end{cases}$$ is a bijection. Hence $|\ZZ| = |\NN|$.
:::

:::proof
The map $f$ sends the nonnegative integers to the even natural numbers and the negative integers to the odd ones ($-1\mapsto 1$, $-2\mapsto 3$, and so on). The map $g : \NN\to\ZZ$ given by $g(m) = m/2$ for even $m$ and $g(m) = -(m+1)/2$ for odd $m$ satisfies $g\circ f = \id_{\ZZ}$ and $f\circ g = \id_{\NN}$, so $f$ is a bijection by Proposition [1.5.5](/notes/math-55a/1-5-inverses-and-composites#proposition-1-5-5).
:::

:::proposition{1.7.4} Pairs of natural numbers
The map $\NN\times\NN\to\NN$, $(k,l)\mapsto 2^k(2l+1)-1$, is a bijection. Consequently $|\NN^n| = |\NN|$ for every $n\ge 1$.
:::

:::proof
Every positive integer $m$ can be written as $m = 2^k(2l+1)$ with $k,l\in\NN$ in exactly one way: $2^k$ must be the largest power of $2$ dividing $m$, and $2l+1$ the odd number $m/2^k$. So $(k,l)\mapsto 2^k(2l+1)$ is a bijection from $\NN\times\NN$ onto the positive integers, and the additional $-1$ shifts the positive integers onto $\NN$; for instance, $(0,0)\mapsto 2^0(2\cdot 0+1)-1 = 0$.

For the second statement we induct on $n$, the case $n = 1$ being trivial. Sending $(x_1,\ldots,x_{n+1})$ to $((x_1,\ldots,x_n),x_{n+1})$ is a bijection $\NN^{n+1}\to\NN^n\times\NN$. If $\beta : \NN^n\to\NN$ is a bijection, then $(u,v)\mapsto(\beta(u),v)$ is a bijection $\NN^n\times\NN\to\NN\times\NN$, with inverse $(a,v)\mapsto(\beta^{-1}(a),v)$, and the first part finishes the induction.
:::

:::proposition{1.7.5} The rationals are countable
$|\QQ| = |\NN|$. More generally, $\ZZ^n$ and $\QQ^n$ are countably infinite for every $n\ge 1$.
:::

:::proof
For $x\in\QQ$, let $b$ be the smallest positive integer such that $bx\in\ZZ$, and send $x$ to the pair $(bx,b)\in\ZZ\times\NN$. This is injective, since $x$ is recovered as $bx/b$. Composing with the bijection $\ZZ\times\NN\to\NN\times\NN$, $(a,b)\mapsto(f(a),b)$, where $f$ is the bijection of Proposition [1.7.3](/notes/math-55a/1-7-cardinality#proposition-1-7-3), and then with the bijection of Proposition [1.7.4](/notes/math-55a/1-7-cardinality#proposition-1-7-4), gives an injection $\QQ\injto\NN$. The inclusion $\NN\subseteq\QQ$ gives an injection the other way, and the Schröder–Bernstein theorem gives $|\QQ| = |\NN|$.

If $\beta : \QQ\to\NN$ is a bijection, then $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\mapsto(\beta(x_1),\ldots,\beta(x_n))$ is a bijection $\QQ^n\to\NN^n$, and $|\NN^n| = |\NN|$ by Proposition [1.7.4](/notes/math-55a/1-7-cardinality#proposition-1-7-4). The same argument applies to $\ZZ^n$.
:::

Not every infinite set is countable. To show this for $\RR$ we use decimal expansions, and one fact about them from analysis: every $t\in[0,1)$ has exactly one decimal expansion $$t = 0.a_0a_1a_2\ldots = \sum_{k\ge 0}a_k10^{-(k+1)}, \qquad a_k\in\{0,1,\ldots,9\},$$ that does not end in an infinite string of $9$s (we exclude, for instance, $0.0999\ldots$, which equals $0.1000\ldots$); and every digit sequence that does not end in an infinite string of $9$s is the expansion of some $t\in[0,1)$. We call this expansion the ***decimal expansion*** of $t$.

:::theorem{1.7.6} Cantor’s diagonal argument
No map $\NN\to\RR$ is surjective. Hence $|\NN|<|\RR|$, and $\RR$ is uncountable.
:::

:::proof
We first show that no map $g : \NN\to[0,1)$ is surjective. Write the decimal expansions of its values one below the other, $$\begin{array}{r@{\;=\;}l}
g(0) & 0.\,\bm{a_{00}}\,a_{01}\,a_{02}\,a_{03}\ldots\\
g(1) & 0.\,a_{10}\,\bm{a_{11}}\,a_{12}\,a_{13}\ldots\\
g(2) & 0.\,a_{20}\,a_{21}\,\bm{a_{22}}\,a_{23}\ldots\\
g(3) & 0.\,a_{30}\,a_{31}\,a_{32}\,\bm{a_{33}}\ldots\\
\multicolumn{2}{c}{\vdots}
\end{array}$$ and go down the diagonal: let $b_j = 5$ if $a_{jj}\neq 5$ and $b_j = 4$ if $a_{jj} = 5$, and let $y = 0.b_0b_1b_2\ldots$. All digits of $y$ are $4$s and $5$s, so $y\in[0,1)$ and this is its decimal expansion. For each $j$, the decimal expansions of $y$ and $g(j)$ differ in the $j$th digit, so $y\neq g(j)$ by uniqueness of decimal expansions. Thus $y$ is not in the range of $g$.

Now let $f : \NN\to\RR$, and define $g : \NN\to[0,1)$ by $g(j) = f(j)$ if $f(j)\in[0,1)$ and $g(j) = 0$ otherwise. Every element of $[0,1)$ in the range of $f$ is in the range of $g$. So the element $y\in[0,1)$ just constructed for $g$, which is not in the range of $g$, is not in the range of $f$ either, and $f$ is not surjective. In particular there is no bijection $\NN\to\RR$, while the inclusion $\NN\subseteq\RR$ gives $|\NN|\le|\RR|$.
:::

The same idea shows that there are arbitrarily large cardinalities.

:::theorem{1.7.7} There is no largest cardinality
For every set $S$, no map $S\to\mcP(S)$ is surjective. Hence $|S|<|\mcP(S)|$.
:::

:::proof
Let $\alpha : S\to\mcP(S)$, and let $A = \{s\in S\mid s\notin\alpha(s)\}$. Suppose $A = \alpha(t)$ for some $t\in S$. Then $t\in A$ if and only if $t\notin\alpha(t) = A$, a contradiction. So $A$ is not in the range of $\alpha$, and there is no bijection $S\to\mcP(S)$. On the other hand, $s\mapsto\{s\}$ is an injection $S\injto\mcP(S)$.
:::

This is the diagonal argument again. Think of a map $\alpha : S\to\mcP(S)$ as a table with rows and columns indexed by $S$, whose entry in row $s$ and column $t$ is $1$ if $t\in\alpha(s)$ and $0$ otherwise. The set $A$ is obtained by going down the diagonal and switching every entry, so it differs from the row of $s$ in column $s$, for every $s$.

By Proposition [1.3.7](/notes/math-55a/1-3-functions#proposition-1-3-7), subsets of $S$ and functions $S\to\{0,1\}$ amount to the same thing: $A\mapsto\chi_A$ is a bijection $\mcP(S)\to\{0,1\}^S$, whose inverse sends $\varphi$ to $\varphi^{-1}(1)$. So $|\{0,1\}^S| = |\mcP(S)|>|S|$. If $S$ is finite with $|S| = n$, a function $S\to\{0,1\}$ makes one of two choices at each of the $n$ elements, so $|\mcP(S)| = 2^n$, and the theorem generalizes the inequality $n<2^n$. Applying the theorem repeatedly produces ever larger sets $S$, $\mcP(S)$, $\mcP(\mcP(S))$, …; so there is no largest cardinality.

Finally, sequences of real numbers are no more numerous than real numbers themselves.

:::proposition{1.7.8} Cardinality of mappings
$|\RR^{\NN}| = |\RR|$.
:::

:::proof
We find injections in both directions and apply the Schröder–Bernstein theorem, working with $[0,1)$ in place of $\RR$.

First, $|\RR| = |[0,1)|$. The inclusion $[0,1)\subseteq\RR$ is an injection one way. For the other, $x\mapsto x/(1+|x|)$ is a strictly increasing, hence injective, map $\RR\to(-1,1)$, and $u\mapsto(u+1)/2$ maps $(-1,1)$ injectively into $(0,1)\subseteq[0,1)$. By the Schröder–Bernstein theorem, there is a bijection $\beta : \RR\to[0,1)$. Applying $\beta$ termwise, $(x_j)_{j\in\NN}\mapsto(\beta(x_j))_{j\in\NN}$, is a bijection $\RR^{\NN}\to[0,1)^{\NN}$, with inverse given by applying $\beta^{-1}$ termwise. So it suffices to show that $|[0,1)^{\NN}| = |[0,1)|$.

The map $t\mapsto(t,0,0,\ldots)$ is an injection $[0,1)\injto[0,1)^{\NN}$. For the other direction we interleave decimal digits. Let $\pi : \NN\times\NN\to\NN$, $\pi(j,k) = 2^j(2k+1)-1$, be the bijection of Proposition [1.7.4](/notes/math-55a/1-7-cardinality#proposition-1-7-4). Given a sequence $(t_j)_{j\in\NN}$ in $[0,1)$, write the decimal expansions $t_j = 0.a_{j0}a_{j1}a_{j2}\ldots$, and define a digit sequence $(c_m)_{m\in\NN}$ by $$c_{\pi(j,k)} = a_{jk};$$ that is, the $k$th digit of $t_j$ is placed in position $\pi(j,k)$. Since $\pi$ is a bijection, every position receives exactly one digit. The positions $\pi(0,k) = 2k$ carry the digits of $t_0$, infinitely many of which differ from $9$; so $(c_m)$ does not end in an infinite string of $9$s, and it is the decimal expansion of some $y\in[0,1)$. If $(t_j)\neq(t'_j)$, then $t_j\neq t'_j$ for some $j$, so their decimal expansions differ in some digit $k$, and the two digit sequences built from them differ in position $\pi(j,k)$; by uniqueness of decimal expansions, the corresponding values of $y$ differ. So $(t_j)\mapsto y$ is an injection $[0,1)^{\NN}\injto[0,1)$.

By the Schröder–Bernstein theorem, $|[0,1)^{\NN}| = |[0,1)|$, and therefore $|\RR^{\NN}| = |[0,1)^{\NN}| = |[0,1)| = |\RR|$.
:::
